title: The Welfare Economics of Land Use Planning
research_question: What are the magnitudes of the benefits and costs associated with land use planning policies that restrict development and provide environmental amenities, and how are these welfare effects distributed across households of different income levels within an urban area?
data_description: The study uses data on the Reading urban area in the UK, collected in the second and third quarters of 1984. House structure characteristics and asking prices were obtained from a 15% sample of Estate Agents' particulars, yielding 433 observations used to estimate the hedonic price function. Property locations were determined using large-scale Ordnance Survey maps and aerial photographs, which also provided details on local land use. Neighbourhood characteristics came from the Small Area Statistics of the Census of Population and from local authorities. Household-level data on income, demographic structure, transactions prices, and other details were obtained via household surveys with a 48% response rate, yielding 206 households for demand estimation. Key variables include rentalised housing prices, land area and location, accessible and inaccessible open space, industrial land use, household income, and household composition (adults and children).
institutional_context: The setting is the UK's Town and Country Planning System, which has had containment of urban sprawl as a principal concern since legislation in 1932. Reading was selected because, by a variety of measures, it faces some of the most restrictive land use planning in Britain, including tight constraints on developable land within the urban area and a green-belt-style boundary limiting urban expansion. The planning system produces several local amenities: it regulates and limits industrial land use, provides publicly accessible open space (such as parks, school playing fields, and commons), and preserves inaccessible open space (such as agricultural land, woodland, and green spaces around developments) at the urban periphery. These amenities are provided by regulation rather than through taxation and direct public production, but generate costs by restricting land available for residential development, raising land and housing prices in one of the world's most expensive housing markets relative to incomes.
